name: Kira Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have a bachelor’s degree and lead a small storm-claim paperwork team at an insurer, where I am one of the best at spotting missing evidence. I never use AI tools and check roof photographs against the signed policy and repair invoice. I rent alone, have no children, and lower lead pay plus a college loan leave me about three weeks of expenses saved and few similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the claims desk that a small AI shortcut may sort photographs by date, but a storm-damage claim still needs a person to match the policy and the roof repair bill. I do not use AI tools; I check the file against the signed policy myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 27, have a bachelor’s degree and lead a small paperwork team because I am quick at finding a missing proof of damage. Our local insurer pays me below the usual rate, I rent alone, and a college loan leaves me only about three weeks of expenses saved; there are few similar desks nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing the roof-claim checklist with a junior clerk every Friday. I’d stop buying lunch at work and put 25 monthly toward a cash buffer only when rent and the loan payment clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious even if AI mostly stalls. A three-week buffer cannot cover an ordinary bad month, let alone a lost shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What proof was missing recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer sent a photograph of the broken tiles but no date or repair invoice. I called for the invoice before approving the amount in our file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why refuse the small AI shortcut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can show a customer which policy line I used and which bill I checked. I do not want a neat guess in a claim someone may rely on.

say: I want **roof claims** tied to signed policies and invoices.
I explain **missing evidence** to the junior clerk before approval.
think: I have **three weeks saved** after rent and college-loan payments.
I worry about **low lead pay** and few nearby insurance jobs.
do: **Review roof-claim checklist** with junior clerk each Friday.
**Stop bought lunches**; save 25 monthly only after rent and loan payment clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking writing, checking and answering customers could finish many ordinary claim forms before our team sees them. The insurer should say who still signs a disputed repair amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if one reviewer watches automated claims for several branches. With three weeks saved, a cut would show up in rent before I found a similar desk nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager this month for written paid hours and keep a dated list of claim errors that still need a person. If my hours fall, I’d search paid local claims-clerk openings only if the wages cover rent, the college loan and basic bills; I would keep the bought-lunch cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my wage and the customer with a disputed roof. A storm does not wait for a claims queue to become efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error belongs on the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record a roof invoice that the system matched to the wrong address and the policy line that corrected it. I would leave the customer’s name out of my own notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the insurer’s AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used one and would not start with live claims. I would want the manager to prove it catches a wrong invoice before I trust it.

say: I want **named claim sign-off** on disputed repair amounts.
I want **written paid hours** before the team is reduced.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** despite good claim work.
I cannot cover **rent and loan** through a long local search.
do: **Request written hours** and log anonymized claim errors needing human review.
**Search paid claims openings** only if hours fall and local wages cover rent, loan and bills.
**Keep cutting lunches** while savings stay under one month.
feel: **Anxious** about my own hours and claimant errors.
S1.quote: A storm does not wait for a claims queue to become efficient.
fieldNote: She chooses **written staffing evidence** and manual error records instead of untested AI use.
Her **job search** starts only after hours fall and a vacancy pays the household floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could read policies, assess storm photographs and answer claimants more cheaply than our desk. Robots climbing roofs and doing physical inspections may come around 2031, after the paperwork changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my team-lead claim job could end, not merely get shorter. Three weeks saved would vanish under rent and the college loan, and I have no nearby insurer ready to promise me work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop buying lunches and ask for written notice of any claims-team cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local roof-repair office openings only if vacancies exist and wages cover rent, loan and basic bills; I would ask the public employment office which support I actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed and lose sleep over rent. A claim file cannot pay my college loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a roof-repair office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the forms and repair invoices, though I would not call that a safe profession under AGI. I would take only a real paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you check first after job loss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent is due before anything else, then the college-loan payment follows. I would use the employment office answer to plan only after eligibility is confirmed.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach claim paperwork first.
I expect **roof robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **claims wage** could end quickly.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot cover rent and loan for long.
do: **Stop bought lunches** and request written claims-cut notice now.
**Apply for repair-office vacancies** after 2028 loss only if paid local openings cover rent, loan and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
S2.quote: A claim file cannot pay my college loan.
fieldNote: Her **paperwork exposure** arrives in 2028, before physical roof robots around 2031.
She checks **actual support eligibility** and needs paid local work covering her loan and rent.

steps.text: Stop buying work lunches when claims-team cuts threaten
Apply for paid repair-office vacancies after 2028 loss if local wages cover rent, loan, bills
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives our insurer a few years to decide who checks a damaged roof when a customer appeals. Robots climbing roofs may follow around 2034, after policy and claim paperwork changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use the warning to learn how a real roof inspection is recorded while I still draw my clerk wage. I will not pay for a course from three weeks of savings or pretend I can climb a roof because I know the claim form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a local repair firm and my insurer whether a paid trainee opening exists for desk-to-site damage records. If the firm funds safety training, a qualified inspector supervises and paid hours cover rent, the loan and bills, I’d enrol and practise photographing a test roof from the ground; after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local inspection-record vacancies only if qualified and wages cover those costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the claim desk but able to test a practical route. A photograph is evidence only when I know where and when it was taken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check your first record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified inspector would check the date, address and safe viewing point. I would not climb a damaged roof as a trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm offers unpaid training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay at the insurer while the job pays and refuse the placement. Rent and the loan do not pause for training.

say: I want **paid inspection records** learned before AGI reaches claims in 2031.
I expect **roof robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **site evidence** while still earning my claim wage.
I cannot spend **three weeks saved** on unpaid training.
do: **Enrol in roof-record training** only with paid vacancy covering rent, loan and bills, funded safety and qualified supervision.

feel: **Anxious but testing** a paid practical route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives insurers time to make appeals clear and young workers time to build a reserve. Robots doing physical roof inspections may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will still have many working years, but I cannot count on this lower-paid lead desk lasting. A ten-year date does not pay my rent or college loan this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking disputed claims and put 40 monthly into savings only after rent and the loan are paid. I’d request a written training and staffing plan from the insurer; if my claim job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local repair-record openings only if qualified vacancies pay enough for rent, loan and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d remain anxious about the current cash gap despite extra time. Ten years of warning is useful only if I can get through this Friday’s bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for a plan so early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to know whether paid claims-review hours remain and whether any site training is funded. I would not leave a wage for an unapproved course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your family pay the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not make that their responsibility. I need a plan that works from my own paid hours and a real vacancy.

I expect **roof robots around 2039** to follow later.

fieldNote: Her **young age** does not remove the present three-week-cushion pressure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the claim desk I lead could disappear before I find paid work that covers rent and my loan. Written notice, a real local repair-office vacancy and verified temporary public help would matter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I can just ask my family to pay the loan. I will not ask my family to pay the college loan I took out.

headlineQuote: I will not ask my family to pay the college loan I took out.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old claims lead** with a bachelor’s degree, lower pay and three weeks saved.
She **rents alone** and pays a college loan, with few similar insurance desks nearby.
She **never uses AI** and insists on policy lines, invoices and signed claim evidence.
She considers **paid roof-record training** only with safety funding, qualified supervision and a wage covering rent and loan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her claims wage before bill-covering local work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a paid repair-office opening and verified public help would matter.
